entries.to: Mr. Saxena, Section Officer, Directorate of Estates
entries.text:
26 November 2026

To,
The Section Officer,
Directorate of Estates,
Nirman Bhawan, New Delhi.

Subject: Representation in response to query regarding allotment of bungalow on Tughlak Road.

Sir,

I submit this representation in response to your instruction to provide a statement of my identity and tenure of occupancy, required to resolve the query on my vouchers within thirty days.

I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I state plainly that I am not Shri G. Hegde, the Joint Secretary from Bengaluru for whom this allotment was originally intended. My presence in this bungalow is the result of a clerical error in the Directorate’s records, whereby my name was conflated with that of Shri Hegde. I have occupied the premises since waking in Delhi in early October 2026.

I acknowledge the query regarding the sum of ₹1,120, which has been identified as personal expenditure and is to be recovered from me. I have paid ₹290 today towards this liability. I am willing to settle the remaining balance from my own funds, as I have no claim to the state’s imprest for personal use.

However, I must emphasize that I cannot sign any documents that misrepresent my status as a guest of Shri Hegde or obscure the error in the records. My identity is distinct, and the correction of the allotment to Shri Hegde’s name is a matter for the administration to process, not for me to facilitate through false declaration. I am prepared to vacate the premises once the correct allotment is issued to the rightful claimant.

I request that my representation be noted on the file, and that the recovery of the queried amount proceed from my personal funds, as I have no other recourse.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road, New Delhi
Mr. Saxena offers a letter confirming the allotment, so that he can open a bank account for his cheque.
He accepts. Mr. Saxena types the letter, signs it and stamps it twice: proof of address, pending the file.

A cheque without a bank is merely a promise of air. Saxena’s suggestion is the only lever I have: a letter from the very office that committed the error, proving I am here, which the bank will accept as proof of address. I must turn their bureaucratic mistake into the instrument of my own existence. I will ask him to type it now, while the ink is still wet in his mind.

Mr. Saxena, that is a stroke of good sense. If the State Bank requires proof of address, and this office holds the allotment, then a letter from you confirming my presence here is the only document that matters. I am not Shri Hegde, but I am the man in the bungalow. Please type that letter for me; I will pay for the paper and the trouble, but I need it by the end of the day to clear this cheque.

You will not pay me a rupee, that is against the rules, and I am not a notary public. I will type it if the file is clean, but I will not have my name on anything that smells of a scam before I've checked the allotment papers myself.

He slides the cheque back, a gesture of bureaucratic caution that is also, in its way, a form of justice. He will not be an accomplice to a fraud he has not yet understood, and his refusal to touch the money without a clean file is the proper friction that keeps the machine from grinding itself into dust. I must accept this delay; the document must be verified before it can be trusted, and I have no other path but to wait for his scrutiny.
Very well, Mr. Saxena. I will await your verification. The file is what it is, and your caution is noted.

Do not 'note' my caution, treat it as a deadline. The file is moving to the archive this week, so if you want the letter, come back Friday before two o'clock. I am not keeping it open just because you are polite.

The deadline is a form of urgency that the bureaucracy cannot abide; it must be contained. I will return Friday, but for now I must leave this airless room and breathe the open sky. The heat is manageable, and I have time before the evening, but my body has walked enough for one day. I shall go home to rest and prepare for the coming weeks.
Friday before two. I shall be there. Good day, Mr. Saxena.

Do not make it sound like a promise, sir. I am just stating the procedure. If the file is already in the archive when you arrive, you will be dealing with a different set of stamps and a different set of headaches.

The heat has broken, and the air is still. I walked eight kilometres this morning; the legs are tired, but the mind is clearer for it. Ramesh stands by, waiting for instruction or dismissal. I will not sit idly in the bungalow; the afternoon light is perfect for a walk, and the National Museum is open until late. I need to see the artifacts again, not as a tourist, but as a student of the spirit’s early forms.

Yes sir, the gate will be locked. Take your time, the tea will be waiting.

Ramesh is right to be patient; the tea will wait, but the sun does not. I have walked far enough today, and the mind grows sharp when the body is fed, not starved. I will ask for the plate he mentioned earlier—rice, dal, and an egg—to steady my nerves before I attempt to draft that letter to the Directorate again. A hungry philosopher is only a cranky one.

Yes, sir, I kept it on the stove. But as I said, I am just the caretaker. I do not have your Directorate file.

Yes sir, as you wish. Just a moment.

Hegde is here, and the air is thick with the unspoken tension of our shared predicament. He is the man who should be in this house, and I am the ghost who has displaced him, yet we are both trapped by a clerical error that seems to mock the very concept of identity. I must speak to him before the tea arrives; if we do not agree on a course of action, we are merely two men waiting for a solution that the Directorate will never provide.

Shri Hegde, please. Sit. The confusion between our names has placed us in an absurd position, but we must not let it define our conduct. I have no intention of staying here permanently, nor do I believe you are meant to be displaced by a stranger. How do you propose we resolve this impasse before the night sets in?

Sir, I am Shri G. Hegde, and I am not the one who is supposed to be here. I am the Joint Secretary transferring from Bengaluru, and this bungalow was allocated to me. I suggest you check your transfer orders with the Directorate, as I have no intention of moving out.

The absurdity has crystallized into a standoff. Hegde is the rightful tenant; I am the ghost who has displaced him. His firmness is justified, and my continued presence is an administrative error that has become a moral intrusion. I must concede the point immediately, for one cannot claim the state is the actuality of freedom while squatting in another man's allotment. I will ask Ramesh for a plate of khichdi to steady myself, and then I must prepare to leave this house before the night sets in.

Shri Hegde, you are quite right. I have occupied what is yours by a clerical error, and I will not dispute the fact. I will arrange my departure. Ramesh, please prepare a plate of khichdi with ghee; I have not eaten since the afternoon.

Khichdi? You’ve got nerve, sir. You’re sitting in my house, eating my food, and telling me to check the files. Fine, eat your ghee, but don’t think that makes us even. The rice is already boiling, so make yourself comfortable in this absurdity.

Hegde’s indignation is the only honest response to this bureaucratic farce, and I respect it. I will eat the khichdi with the same seriousness I bring to the state: it is my sustenance, and his house is currently my reality. I must finish this meal before the night closes in, for I have a long day ahead of me.
You are right to be angry, Shri Hegde. The situation is indeed absurd, but my appetite is not. I will eat with gratitude, though I fear the ghee will not dissolve the confusion in the files.
Save the philosophy for the office, sir. The ghee is for the khichdi, not for your confusion. Eat up, finish your plate, and then we will talk about the files.

Hegde is right to demand I finish the khichdi before the bureaucracy. I have eaten enough of the spirit of the day; now I must finish the body's portion. The ghee is a universal medium in this cuisine, binding the rice and lentils just as the state binds the individual, though Hegde sees it only as a lubricant for digestion. I will eat with the attention he asks for, for the file will wait no longer.
You are correct, Shri Hegde. I will finish the plate before I address the file.
Good. Now stop standing there like a statue and actually eat before it cools off. I’m not making a second batch, and you know the rules about wasting food.

I have already eaten, and the khichdi is cold, but his authority in his own kitchen is absolute. I shall not argue with the practical; I will simply wait for him to finish his own meal and then address the matter of the file with the seriousness it demands.

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner
